unit.title: The Real Price of Fast Fashion
objectives: I can explain hidden costs described in a text.
I can use the passive voice and concession words.
I can write an opinion paragraph with evidence.

passages.title: The Real Price of Fast Fashion

paragraphs: Walk into any shopping mall and you will find stores that release new collections almost every week. This business model, known as fast fashion, allows consumers to buy trendy clothing at remarkably low prices. For many teenagers, it means they can follow the latest styles without spending a month's allowance.

However, the low price on the tag hides a much higher cost. Producing a single cotton T-shirt can require around 2,700 liters of water, roughly what one person drinks in two and a half years. Factories that dye fabrics often release chemicals into nearby rivers, and many garment workers, most of them women, earn wages that are barely enough to survive.

The problem continues after we buy the clothes. Because fast-fashion items are designed to be cheap rather than durable, they wear out quickly, and millions of tons of textiles end up in landfills each year. Although donating old clothes seems like a solution, charities receive far more garments than they can resell, so many are shipped overseas or burned.

Some designers and shoppers are now pushing back. Second-hand markets, clothing-swap events, and repair workshops are becoming popular among young people who want to express their style without harming the planet. Their message is simple: the most sustainable piece of clothing is the one already hanging in your closet.
Many clothing stores sell new clothes almost every week. This is called fast fashion. The clothes are cheap and look modern. Teenagers can buy new styles without spending too much money.

But cheap clothes have hidden costs. Making one cotton T-shirt can use about 2,700 liters of water. That is about how much one person drinks in two and a half years. Some factories put dirty chemicals into rivers. Many garment workers get very low pay.

There are more problems after we buy the clothes. Fast-fashion clothes are cheap, so they are not durable. Every year, millions of tons of old clothes go into landfills. Giving old clothes away sounds good. But charities get too many clothes, so many are sent to other countries or burned.

Now some young people want to change this. They buy used clothes, swap clothes with friends, and learn to fix them. Their idea is simple: the most sustainable clothes are the ones already in your closet.

glossary.example: The factory makes 1,000 garments a day.
These boots are durable; I have worn them for five years.
Riding a bike is a sustainable way to travel.

questions.stem: Which sentence best summarizes the passage?

options.text: Fast fashion is cheap for shoppers but costly for people and the planet.
Fast fashion helps teenagers save money every month.
options.feedback: That is only the first paragraph. What about paragraphs 2–4?

options.text: Charities should sell more second-hand clothes.
options.feedback: Charities appear only in paragraph 3 as one detail.

options.text: Cotton T-shirts are better than other clothes.
options.feedback: The T-shirt is an example of hidden costs, not a recommendation.

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts low prices (P1) with hidden costs (P2–P3) and ends with alternatives (P4). A summarizes this contrast.

hints.text: Paragraph 2 begins with "However". What changes after this word?
Key words: "low price on the tag hides a much higher cost".
Options C and D are small details, not a summary.
A summary must cover the whole text: cheap price vs. hidden costs. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Why does the writer compare the water used for one T-shirt with what a person drinks?

options.text: To make a large number easier to imagine
To encourage people to drink more water
options.feedback: The paragraph is about the cost of clothes, not health.

options.text: To show that cotton needs no water
options.feedback: It is the opposite — cotton needs a lot of water.

questions.explanation: 2,700 liters is hard to picture; "two and a half years of drinking water" makes the amount real to readers.

hints.text: Find "2,700 liters" in paragraph 2.
Can you imagine 2,700 liters? Is "two and a half years of drinking" easier to imagine?
Option C is the opposite of the text.
Writers use comparisons to make numbers easy to picture. Answer: A.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about donating old clothes?

options.text: It completely solves the problem of textile waste.
options.feedback: The text says it only "seems like" a solution.

options.text: It does not always keep clothes out of the waste stream.
Charities refuse to accept any clothes.
options.feedback: Charities receive MANY clothes — too many.

options.text: Donated clothes are always resold locally.
options.feedback: Many are shipped overseas or burned.

questions.explanation: "Seems like a solution" + "many are shipped overseas or burned" → donating does not always prevent waste.

hints.text: Look at the last sentence of paragraph 3.
Key words: "seems like a solution", "shipped overseas or burned".
words: sent to other countries or burned

hints.text: Options A and D use "completely" and "always" — extreme words are often wrong.
"Seems" means it is not really a full solution. Answer: B.

questions.stem: What is the writer's attitude toward second-hand markets and repair workshops?

options.feedback: Is there any negative word about them in paragraph 4?
The writer ends the whole passage with them — that shows interest.

questions.explanation: The writer presents them as a positive way to "express their style without harming the planet" and ends with their message.

hints.text: Read paragraph 4. Are the words positive or negative?
Key words: "without harming the planet", "most sustainable".
Nothing in paragraph 4 sounds angry.
Positive words → supportive attitude. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Millions of tons of textiles ___ (throw) away every year.
questions.explanation: Textiles 不會自己丟掉 → 被動語態 be + p.p.；every year 是現在簡單式，主詞複數 → are thrown.

hints.text: Do textiles throw themselves away, or are they thrown by people?
Passive voice: be + past participle (p.p.).
"Every year" → present tense. "Textiles" is plural → are. The p.p. of throw is thrown.
Answer: are thrown.

questions.stem: ___ donating clothes seems helpful, many garments are still burned.

options.feedback: "Helpful" and "burned" are opposite ideas. Because shows a reason, not a contrast.
"So" shows a result and cannot start this kind of sentence.

questions.explanation: 兩個子句意思相反（helpful ↔ burned）→ 讓步連接詞 Although.

hints.text: Are the two ideas similar or opposite?
Opposite ideas → although / though / even though.
Option C cannot begin this clause.
Answer: Although.

questions.stem: Should teenagers buy fewer new clothes? Write a paragraph with two reasons and one piece of evidence from the article.

scaffolds.model_text: I believe teenagers should buy fewer new clothes. One reason is that fast fashion has hidden costs for the planet. According to the article, one cotton T-shirt can use about 2,700 liters of water. Another reason is that cheap clothes are not durable, so they quickly end up in landfills. Although new styles are fun, we can still express ourselves by swapping or buying second-hand clothes. In conclusion, buying less is a simple way to protect the environment.
checklist: I used one piece of evidence from the article.
I used at least one linking word (Although, Another, In conclusion).
I checked spelling and verb tenses.

questions.explanation: Strong opinion writing uses evidence from a source, not only personal feelings.

hints.text: Choose your position. Then look back at paragraph 2 or 3 for evidence.
Use "According to the article, ..." to add evidence. See the sentence frames.
Sample: "According to the article, millions of tons of textiles end up in landfills each year."
Read the model paragraph, then write your own version.
